target.title: Fully Implanted Brain–Computer Interface in a Locked-In Patient with ALS
target.venue: The New England Journal of Medicine (N Engl J Med)
target.version: Author manuscript; published in final edited form as N Engl J Med. 2016;375(21):2060–2066

read.pdf: Figs. 1–3 captions; no tables in text.txt

entries.text: The authors report a home-use communication system combining a totally implanted BCI with automated decoding and typing software for one locked-in patient with ALS.
entries.condition: Single patient with late-stage ALS; system included implanted subdural electrodes and an implanted thoracic transmitter, plus external antenna, receiver, tablet, and typing software.
entries.quote: We report on a communication system that involves a totally implantable brain–computer interface for home use by a locked-in patient with ALS.

entries.text: The abstract reports controlled typing at the equivalent of two letters per minute 28 weeks after electrode placement.
entries.condition: One patient; by attempting to move the hand contralateral to the implanted electrodes; reported 28 weeks after electrode placement.
entries.quote: at the equivalent of two letters per minute.

entries.text: The abstract places the reported typing performance at 28 weeks after electrode placement.
entries.condition: Single patient; typing through the commercial spelling program using brain-click selection.

entries.text: The participant was a 58-year-old woman with late-stage ALS, locked-in and mechanically ventilated.
entries.condition: One woman; consent obtained September 2015; late-stage ALS, tracheostomy with positive-pressure ventilation, otherwise completely paralyzed.

entries.text: Four subdural electrode strips were implanted; each had four 4-mm electrodes at 1-cm interelectrode spacing, with two strips over each of two target regions.
entries.unit: count; count; electrode diameter; interelectrode distance; count
entries.condition: Implantation on day 0 (October 27, 2015); targets were left motor hand region and left prefrontal region.
entries.loc: Methods: Implantation and Description of Electrodes and Device

entries.text: Temporary externalized electrocorticography was sampled at 512 Hz and filtered from 0.15 to 134.4 Hz before two strips were connected to the implanted Activa PC+S amplifier/transmitter.
entries.unit: Hz sampling rate; Hz filter passband
entries.condition: Temporary connection after implantation; the permanent implanted device was connected three days later to two electrode strips.
entries.quote: temporary connection to electrocorticography equipment (Micromed; sampling rate, 512 Hz; high-pass filter at 0.15 Hz and low-pass filter at 134.4 Hz).
entries.loc: Methods: Implantation and Description of Electrodes and Device

entries.text: The strip over the left sensorimotor hand area was selected because it produced the best early signals and consistent BCI control; the prefrontal target was retained as backup.
entries.condition: fMRI guided targeting; electrocorticography used for strip selection; electrodes e2 and e3 chosen for feedback; results reported only for sensorimotor activation.
entries.loc: Methods: Determination of Activated Cortical Region

entries.text: The two implantation procedures lasted 6.75 hours and 1.5 hours.
entries.condition: Two procedures under general anesthesia in the single patient.
entries.loc: Methods: Implantation and Description of Electrodes and Device

entries.text: For 28 weeks the team tested and improved decoding algorithms and parameters; settings yielding good control were fixed, after which the patient practiced controlling her signal.
entries.condition: One patient; task-based algorithm/parameter testing and practice; parameter settings were later fixed for the rest of the study.

entries.text: Target-task practice used attempted right-hand movement to move a cursor upward and relaxation to move it downward.
entries.condition: One patient; visual cursor task; target task was used for practice and parameter/algorithm testing.

entries.text: The ball task trained regulation of brain-signal magnitude and timing and was used only to adjust parameters, not after settings were fixed.
entries.condition: One patient; ball moved up/down at computer-indicated times; task was not retained for post-calibration training.

entries.text: The click task trained the patient to select highlighted items by withholding a hand-movement-associated brain click until the intended item was highlighted.
entries.condition: One patient; items presented in rows and columns; intended brain click was attempted hand movement for approximately one second.

entries.text: Spelling selected individual or grouped letters by brain clicks while letters were highlighted automatically and sequentially; performance was tested on dictated words.
entries.condition: One patient; user withheld clicks until the desired letter/group; research spelling task used dictated words.

entries.text: The patient completed 67 home sessions, two per week and two hours each, over 262 days after surgery; training and home-use sessions overlapped for several weeks.
entries.condition: Single patient at home; sessions included algorithm testing, system-stability assessment, and spelling practice.

entries.text: Across the 67 sessions, 357 task runs were performed, with individual tasks lasting 2 to 5 minutes.
entries.condition: Single patient; task runs across the training-session schedule at home.

entries.text: Target-task accuracy averaged 91% with SD 6 percentage points over 83 runs from post-implant days 15–262.
entries.condition: One patient; target task; 83 runs, days 15–262; no independent held-out test partition is described.
entries.quote: The patient’s performance on the target task was correct a mean (±SD) of 91±6% of the time (83 runs were performed between day 15 and day 262).

entries.text: Click-task accuracy averaged 87% with SD 7 percentage points over 37 runs from post-implant days 157–238.
entries.condition: One patient; click task; 37 runs, days 157–238; software settings were fixed at day 157.

entries.text: Suppressing unintended clicks while retaining sensitivity to intended clicks required several months of algorithm refinement; parameter testing ended on day 157 and settings were then fixed.
entries.condition: Single-patient click control; settings fixed for the remainder of the study after parameter testing.
entries.quote: Inhibiting unintended brain clicks while preserving sensitivity to intended actions required several months of refining the algorithms.

entries.text: Spelling accuracy averaged 89% with SD 6 percentage points over 44 research-visit runs from post-implant days 168–262.
entries.condition: One patient; dictated-word spelling by brain-click selection; 44 runs during research visits, days 168–262; correct responses included active and inactive trials.
entries.quote: From day 168 to day 262, a total of 44 spelling runs were performed during research visits, and the patient’s performance was correct 89±6% of the time
entries.loc: Results: Communication and Independent Home Use

entries.loc: Results: Communication and Independent Home Use

questions.q: What do the headline accuracy and speed figures actually measure, and under what conditions?
questions.answer: They are online, repeated task-run outcomes for one patient: target task 91±6% over 83 runs, click task 87±7% over 37 runs, and dictated-word spelling 89±6% over 44 research-visit runs. Typing rate was two letters per minute at 28 weeks; the later 33 seconds per letter was reported with word prediction. No independent held-out test split or chance baseline is described.

questions.q: How independent was home communication in practice?
questions.answer: The participant used the system on 32 days during the day-197-to-266 logging period, averaging 86 minutes per day, and relied on it outdoors when eye tracking failed. The system still required assistance positioning the antenna and setting up the external receiver, tablet, and cables.

questions.q: What most limits claims of generalizable accuracy or superiority over conventional communication?
questions.answer: This is a single-patient case report with iterative parameter tuning and no reported independent test partition, random-seed protocol, chance baseline, or controlled performance comparator. The authors identify cortical damage, cognitive impairment, and unsupportive caregiving as possible limits for future users; they do not claim comparative performance superiority over eye tracking.
